Getting Started with circuitscaper

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

What is circuit-theory connectivity?

Landscape connectivity — how easily organisms, genes, or ecological processes can move across a landscape — is central to spatial ecology and conservation biology. Circuit theory offers a powerful way to model it. The idea is to treat a landscape as an electrical circuit: each raster cell is a node, adjacent cells are connected by resistors, and current flowing through the network reveals movement patterns. Unlike least-cost path methods, which find only the single cheapest route, circuit theory considers all possible pathways simultaneously. This makes it especially effective at identifying movement corridors and pinch points — places where connectivity is funneled through narrow gaps.

circuitscaper brings circuit-theory connectivity to R, with two families of methods that take the same inputs (terra rasters) and run in the same Julia session:

  • Circuitscape and Omniscape (cs_*() and os_*() functions). The established tools, run through the Circuitscape.jl and Omniscape.jl Julia packages. Results are the same as running those tools directly.
  • Dipole methods (dp_*() functions). circuitscaper’s own methods, which factor one circuit and solve many superposed source–sink pairs (“dipoles”) against it. They cover similar questions — pairwise and omnidirectional connectivity, and connectivity between two distributions — much faster and with a built-in error estimate, but they compute a related, different quantity (squared rather than absolute current) and are stochastic. They are experimental: new, not yet published, and their interface may change.

This vignette covers installation, inputs and how to choose a method. Two articles on the package website go further:

  • Circuitscape and Omniscape: each mode and its options.
  • Dipole methods: how to use them, how they work, and how they compare.

Installation

circuitscaper requires Julia (>= 1.10). The cs_*() and os_*() functions also need the Circuitscape and Omniscape Julia packages; the dipole methods need only Julia. You can install everything from R:

install.packages("circuitscaper")

library(circuitscaper)

# First time only: install Julia and required packages
cs_install_julia()

# Or, if you'll only use the dipole methods: Julia alone, which is
# quicker to install and to start
cs_install_julia(circuitscape = FALSE)

cs_install_julia() downloads the official Julia release for your platform from julialang.org into circuitscaper’s own data directory, so it doesn’t touch any other Julia you have installed. You can add the Circuitscape and Omniscape packages later by running cs_install_julia() again.

If you already have Julia installed, cs_setup() will find it automatically, searching the JULIA_HOME and JULIA_BINDIR environment variables, a Julia installed by cs_install_julia(), and your PATH. If Julia is somewhere else, you can point to it:

cs_setup(julia_home = "/path/to/julia/bin")

Julia starts the first time you call a circuitscaper function, or when you call cs_setup(), and takes a few seconds. The first cs_*() or os_*() call of a session then also loads Circuitscape and Omniscape and warms them up, which takes longer (often 15 seconds or more); the dipole methods skip that step. To use several threads, which speeds up Omniscape and the dipole methods, call cs_setup(threads = ) at the start of your session:

cs_setup(threads = 4)

Key inputs

The resistance surface

Every analysis starts with a resistance surface — a raster where each cell’s value represents how difficult it is for the organism or process of interest to move through that location. These are typically derived from land cover or habitat suitability models. For example, a resistance surface for a forest-dwelling mammal might assign low values to forest (easy to traverse), moderate values to grassland, and high values to urban areas or water. (Note that while the Circuitscape.jl Julia library allows resistance datasets to be specified as adjacency graph networks, circuitscaper currently only supports rasters.)

Resistance values must be positive. If your data represents conductance (ease of movement) rather than resistance, set resistance_is = "conductances". Circuitscape and the dipole methods treat a conductance of zero as no connection, but Omniscape requires all values to be positive in either case. To make cells impassable, set them to NA.

Focal nodes

The focal-node methods (cs_pairwise(), cs_one_to_all(), cs_all_to_one() and dp_pairwise()) require focal nodes — the sites between which you want to measure connectivity. These are typically habitat patches, populations, protected areas, or sampling locations. You can provide them as:

  • A matrix or data.frame of x/y coordinates (simplest)
  • A raster with positive integer IDs at each site (0 and NA are ignored)

Source strength

The omnidirectional methods (os_run() and dp_omni()) need no focal nodes: every cell can be a source, weighted by its source strength, such as habitat quality or suitability. By default both use the conductance surface (the inverse of resistance). For connectivity between two distributions, dp_flux(), dp_omni(destination = ) and dp_directionality() take two surfaces: an origin and a destination.

Choosing a method

Start from the question you’re asking:

Question Circuitscape and Omniscape Dipole methods
How well connected are these sites to each other, and through where? cs_pairwise() dp_pairwise()
How does current spread out from, or converge on, each site? cs_one_to_all(), cs_all_to_one()
How does movement flow between a defined source area and a destination? cs_advanced()
Where are the corridors and barriers across the whole landscape? os_run() dp_omni()
How does movement link two distributions (such as seasonal ranges, or present and future habitat), and which way does it flow? os_run() with os_condition(future = ), for climate dp_flux(), dp_omni(destination = ), dp_directionality()

Pairwise analyses treat discrete sites (habitat patches, populations) and ask how well they’re connected to each other. cs_pairwise() also returns the matrix of effective resistances between sites, a distance measure for analyses such as isolation by resistance in population genetics.

One-to-all and all-to-one modes inject current at each site in turn (or ground each in turn), emphasizing how current disperses from, or converges on, each site — useful for recolonization potential, or finding the most reachable sites.

Advanced mode gives full control over where current enters and leaves: explicit source and ground rasters, and one circuit solved.

Omnidirectional analyses need no focal nodes. They map connectivity continuously across the landscape among all habitat within a dispersal radius, to identify corridors and barriers across the full extent.

Two-distribution analyses ask how movement links one distribution to another: present and future habitat under climate change, breeding and wintering ranges, foraging and roosting habitat, or source populations and restoration sites. dp_flux() maps the net flow from origin to destination, with its direction; dp_omni() with a destination maps the routes between them without direction; and dp_directionality() maps both, with their ratio, showing where movement is one-way and where it runs both ways. For climate change, os_condition() offers a related Omniscape analysis, restricting connections to sources and targets with compatible present and future conditions.

Circuitscape and Omniscape, or dipole methods?

Where both families answer a question, choose by what you need:

  • Circuitscape and Omniscape are established and published, so results compare directly with the many studies that use them. They also offer outputs the dipole methods don’t: pairwise resistance matrices, voltage and per-pair maps, short-circuit regions and conditional connectivity.
  • Dipole methods are much faster on large grids, with many focal nodes, or when you want many runs (several radii, species or scenarios). They treat every habitat cell as a source without block sizes or windows, and each map comes with an estimate of its own noise. But their maps are of squared current over the whole circuit, which ranks cells similarly to Circuitscape and Omniscape but isn’t the same quantity, and they carry some sampling noise. See the Dipole methods article before relying on them.

A first look 

library(terra)
library(circuitscaper)

resistance <- rast(system.file("extdata/resistance.tif", package = "circuitscaper"))

# Pairwise Circuitscape among four sites
sites <- matrix(c(10, 40, 40, 40, 10, 10, 40, 10), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
pw <- cs_pairwise(resistance, sites)
plot(pw$current_map)
pw$resistance_matrix

# Omnidirectional connectivity: Omniscape and the dipole method
os <- os_run(resistance, radius = 10)
dp <- dp_omni(resistance, radius = 10, seed = 1)
plot(c(os$normalized_current, dp$normalized_current))

Saving outputs and other tips

  • CRS preservation: circuitscaper reattaches your input raster’s CRS to outputs.
  • Conductance input: If your surface represents ease of movement rather than difficulty, set resistance_is = "conductances" to avoid inverting values manually.
  • Output files: The cs_*() and os_*() functions write intermediate files to a temporary directory and clean up. To keep them (ASC rasters, INI configuration and resistance matrices), use output_dir.
  • Verbose output: Set verbose = TRUE in the cs_*() and os_*() functions to see the solver’s progress, useful for debugging or monitoring long runs.
